prompt.context: Your client is Petvascent, a pharmaceutical company that makes drugs for pets. One of the client's leading products is Clean Heart, a drug given to dogs with heart worms, has recently suffered declining sales. Petvascent has hired our firm to determine what the problem is and restore sales growth. Clean Heart is taken weekly for one year once prescribed. Petvascent's patent on Clean Heart expires in 2020. There are other medications on the market for heart worms, but none is as effective as Clean Heart. There have been no changes in the proportion of dogs diagnosed with heart worms. Petvascent has an exclusive distribution agreement with PetCo, a national pet store chain, and also sells to vets so they can provide an initial dose to patients, who are then 95% more likely to purchase Clean Heart in stores. However, PetCo has recently complained that Clean Heart is available at other pet stores at a lower price, a clear violation of the exclusive distribution agreement.
prompt.question: What is causing declining sales of Clean Heart, and what should Petvascent do to restore sales growth?

clarifying_info.q: Are there any changes in the competitive landscape?
clarifying_info.a: Two new entrants appeared in 2005, but neither has grown significantly. No competitor has made significant improvements to their drugs.

clarifying_info.q: Has the price of Clean Heart changed?
clarifying_info.a: No changes in price to PetCo or vets.

clarifying_info.q: Has anything changed with marketing or packaging?
clarifying_info.a: No changes to marketing in quality or type; no changes to packaging.
Petvascent sells exclusively to PetCo (retail) and to vets for initial doses.

clarifying_info.q: Have there been changes in pet ownership or vet visit rates?
clarifying_info.a: Pet owners continue to own dogs at similar rates and take pets to vets at the same rates.

exhibits.title: Revenues from heart worm drugs by Competitor
exhibits.shows: A bar/line chart showing revenues (in $ millions) from heart worm drugs for Petvascent (the client) and competitors A through I from 2000 to 2011, with a table of annual growth rates for the overall market and the client
exhibits.data: Market growth rates: positive 2001-2007, turns negative 2008 (-4.36%), near-zero 2009-2010, -1.66% in 2011. Client growth rates: positive 2001-2007, turns negative 2008 (-4.69%), -0.91% in 2009, -1.06% in 2010, -1.76% in 2011. Client revenue is the largest bar. Competitors A-I are smaller players.

exhibits.title: Petvascent's Unit Sales of Clean Heart by Distribution
exhibits.shows: A stacked or grouped bar chart showing Petvascent's annual unit sales of Clean Heart split between Vet Units and PetCo Units
exhibits.data: Scale runs from 0 to 45,000,000 units. Vet Units and PetCo Units are tracked separately by year. In 2009: Vet Units ~15,000,000, PetCo Units ~22,000,000. In 2010: Vet Units ~18,000,000, PetCo Units ~20,000,000.

framework: Pet Owners: trends in pet ownership, frequency of vet visits, proportion diagnosed with heart worms, adherence to treatment, willingness to pay, seeking cheaper alternatives
Vets: prescription rate of Clean Heart vs. alternatives, relations with Petvascent, affordability concerns, quantity ordered from Petvascent
Drug Companies / Competitors: new entrants, improvements in competing drugs, changes in marketing or pricing
PetCo: observed unit sales trend, pricing ($20/unit retail), online presence, display/marketing changes, compliance with exclusive agreement
Petvascent: unit sales by channel, wholesale pricing to PetCo ($17/unit) vs. vets ($10/unit), marketing spend, patent status, packaging

questions.prompt: [Exhibit 1] What does this chart indicate about Petvascent's position in the market?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify: (1) Petvascent is the market leader by revenue. (2) From 2008-2011, Petvascent's revenue declines faster than the overall market, dragging market size down. (3) Two new entrants appeared in 2005 but neither grew significantly. (4) Bonus: Other competitors appear fairly stable, indicating no competitor is stealing share from Petvascent — the problem is internal, not competitive.

questions.prompt: [Exhibit 2] Estimate 2009 and 2010 profits. What is the % change in profit level?
questions.guidance: Candidate must read unit volumes from Exhibit 2, calculate revenue by channel, sum variable costs, add fixed costs, and derive profit for each year and the % change. Allow reasonable estimates from the chart. Candidate should not need to be prompted to find % change — subtract points if they do.

math.setup: Revenue = (Vet Units × $10) + (PetCo Units × $17). Variable costs = $5 raw materials + $0.50 packaging + $1.00 transportation = $6.50/unit. Fixed costs: Marketing $100M (2009), $110M (2010); SG&A $50M (2009), $55M (2010).

questions.prompt: Why would vet purchases increase so much while PetCo unit sales decline?
questions.guidance: Candidate should connect the dots: vets are buying large quantities at the low wholesale price ($10/unit) and reselling to other pet stores, which then sell at $17/unit — undercutting PetCo's retail price of $20/unit. This violates PetCo's exclusive distribution agreement and explains why Clean Heart is appearing at other stores at a lower price. Re-selling by vets is a grey area legally and is not illegal if the box is not clearly labeled 'Not for Resale'.

questions.prompt: Knowing that vets are re-selling to other pet stores, what steps should Petvascent take? What are the risks of those steps?
questions.guidance: Strong answers identify multiple options: (1) Add 'Not for Resale' to packaging — low disruption, clear signal; (2) Change purchase/sales contracts with vets to prohibit resale — more enforceable but risks alienating vet relationships; (3) Limit purchase quantities by vets — reduces leakage but may frustrate legitimate vet needs. Risks: new sales contracts may alienate vets who are important customers and advocates; customers at other stores may have grown accustomed to the lower price and resist returning to PetCo's higher price point.

brainstorming.prompt: What steps can Petvascent take to prevent vets from reselling Clean Heart to other retailers, and what are the risks?

categories.name: Packaging / Labeling
ideas: Add 'Not for Resale' label to all vet-channel packaging
Use distinct packaging for vet channel vs. retail channel to make resale traceable

categories.name: Contractual / Legal
ideas: Revise vet purchase agreements to include anti-resale clauses
Pursue legal action against vets found reselling
Audit vet purchase volumes and flag anomalies

categories.name: Pricing / Channel
ideas: Re-evaluate wholesale pricing to vets to reduce arbitrage margin
Introduce tiered pricing based on order volume
Consider direct-to-consumer channels to reduce reliance on PetCo

categories.name: Relationship Management
ideas: Communicate directly with vets about the issue before taking punitive steps
Strengthen partnership with PetCo to enforce exclusivity

categories.name: Risks
ideas: Alienating vets who are key advocates driving 95% of patient retention
Customers who buy at other stores at $17 may resist PetCo's $20 price
Punitive measures could damage Petvascent's reputation in the vet community

recommendation: Petvascent's revenue decline is driven by vets purchasing Clean Heart at wholesale prices ($10/unit) and reselling it to competing retailers who undercut PetCo's price ($17 vs. $20), violating the exclusive distribution agreement

Recommended actions: (1) Immediately add 'Not for Resale' to vet-channel packaging; (2) Revise vet purchase contracts to prohibit resale; (3) Implement purchase quantity limits for vets to prevent bulk arbitrage
risks: New sales contracts and quantity limits may alienate vets, who are critical customer advocates driving the 95% retention rate
Customers who have grown accustomed to purchasing at lower-priced competing stores may resist returning to PetCo at a higher price
Aggressive enforcement could damage Petvascent's relationship with the vet community
next_steps: Re-evaluate price elasticity of demand for Clean Heart to understand impact of price differential on consumer behavior
Initiate discussions with vets to communicate policy changes diplomatically before enforcement
Work with PetCo to enforce exclusive distribution agreement and address pricing strategy
